To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) outcomes-focused management can be held to account by means of a new ‘man for results’ accountability bargain, which is based on an understanding of what it means to be a ‘man of results’; (2) the new accountability bargain is based on the idea that a manager is accountable for the quality of his account of policy and management outcomes, as well as for his record of delivering efficient outcomes; and (3) the quality of the ‘account of policy outcomes’ is measured
‘managing for results’ is a more appropriate term than ‘managing for outputs’, and that ‘managing for accountability’ is a more useful phrase than ‘managing accountability’.
(a) managers must be held accountable for outcomes, and (b) they can be held accountable for the quality of their ‘accounts’ of outcomes, as well as for the outcomes themselves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the public sector can be held accountable for outcomes.
how managers can be held accountable for the outcomes of their policies and programmes.
the following question: What is a manager accountable for?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘managing for outcome’ accountability is possible, and is worth trying.
the accountability bargain is a ‘win-win’ one.
‘Managing for outcomes is a good thing, but it is not a panacea for all the ills of public sector performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to hold managers accountable for outcomes without losing sight of the need for efficient and effective delivery.

the new accountability bargain requires that managers provide a theory of how their policy or program will work, then show that they have implemented the theory, and then demonstrate that the program or policy is achieving its intended results.
‘managing for outputs’ is a necessary but not sufficient condition for ‘managing for results’.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a more sophisticated approach to outcomes-focused accountability can be developed and that it can be done so with the tools already at hand.
outcomes-focused management is not just about ‘doing’ but also about ‘saying’; and that the ‘saying’ must be done with care.
managers can and do give accounts of policy thrust, but that these accounts are often not well enough developed to be useful in accountability settings.
